The word divan has several distinct meanings. They don't all connect to each other in an obvious way, so the best approach is to learn each one separately.
1. A Type of Bed (Most Common Modern Use)

In everyday modern English — especially in British English — a divan most often refers to a type of bed.

A divan bed consists of two parts: a thick, padded, upholstered base (meaning the base is covered in fabric and is soft to the touch) and a mattress that sits on top of it. The base itself is solid and box-shaped — it sits directly on the floor or on small, short legs. There is usually no headboard or footboard (the tall panels at the head and foot of a traditional bed frame), though a headboard can be added separately.

What makes a divan bed practical is that the base often doubles as storage — it can have drawers built into its sides, so you can store bedding, clothes, or other items inside the bed base itself.

In short, if you picture a neat, low bed where the "box" underneath the mattress is fully padded and covered in fabric, that is a divan bed.
2. A Type of Couch or Sofa

A divan is also a long, low, cushioned seat — essentially a couch or sofa — but one that is typically without a back, or with a back only at one end.

Think of it as a heavily padded, elongated bench. You can sit on it normally, or stretch out and lie down on it like a daybed. It is associated with a relaxed, lounging style of seating. You will often see this type of furniture described in older literature and in homes with Middle Eastern, South Asian, or Ottoman-inspired interior styles, where low seating close to the ground is traditional.

The key features that distinguish a divan couch from a regular sofa:

  • It tends to sit low to the ground.
  • It often has no back, or a very low one, so it can be used from any direction.
  • It is meant for both sitting and reclining.
3. A Council of State (Historical and Political)

In the Ottoman Empire and several other historical Middle Eastern and South Asian states, the Divan (sometimes spelled Diwan) referred to the supreme governing council of the state.

This was the body of the most powerful ministers and advisors who managed the day-to-day administration of the empire on behalf of the ruler (the Sultan, in the Ottoman case). They would gather regularly to discuss affairs of state: military matters, legal judgments, finances, and so on. Decisions made by the Divan carried enormous authority.

The word also referred to the physical place — the hall or chamber — where this council met and held its sessions.

So when you read in a history book that "the matter was brought before the Divan," it means it was brought before the highest governing body of that empire, similar to how we might say something was decided by the Cabinet or the Council of Ministers today.

In Persian, Turkish, Urdu, and Arabic literary traditions, a Divan (also spelled Diwan) is a collected volume of poems by a single poet.

This is not just any anthology — it is specifically a poet's own body of work gathered into one book. Traditionally, the poems in a divan are arranged alphabetically by the final rhyming sound of each poem, rather than by theme or date of composition.

A divan typically contains lyrical poetry — ghazals, qasidas, and other classical verse forms. Writing a complete divan was considered a major literary achievement, and the great classical poets are known precisely by their divans.

Some of the most celebrated divans in world literature:

  • Divan-e-Hafiz — the collected poems of the 14th-century Persian poet Hafez. It is so revered in Iran that many people use it for a practice called fal — opening it to a random page to seek guidance, almost like an oracle.
  • Divan-e-Shams — a vast collection of ecstatic lyrical poetry by the 13th-century Persian poet Rumi, named in honour of his spiritual teacher Shams of Tabriz.

If you hear someone say "she has compiled her divan," it means she has assembled her life's poetry into a single definitive collection.

ContextWhat "divan" means

To summarize simply:

  • In a furniture shop or a home context: a divan is either a padded bed base with a mattress, or a low backless couch for lounging.
  • In historical writing about the Ottoman Empire or similar states: a divan is the imperial governing council, or the room where it met.
  • In the context of Persian, Turkish, or Urdu literature: a divan is a poet's complete collection of poems.

The furniture meanings are what you will encounter most often in everyday life. The historical and literary meanings matter most when reading about Middle Eastern or South Asian history, or classical poetry from that tradition.
